demo.title: Asking is not the same as being allowed.
demo.intro: An illustration that runs in your browser and is connected to nothing. Start the request and watch where it stops. It will not go any further until you approve that exact revision yourself.
demo.approvalLabel: Your approval covers only the target, operation and revision shown above.
demo.halt: Stopped here. The flow is waiting for a human decision and will not continue on its own.
demo.legend: Refused · Waiting for a person · Passed
demo.initial: DENIED · production/payment-api sits outside staging/*, and nobody has approved it.
demo.denied: DENIED · This action is outside the standing scope, or it no longer matches the approval on file. It stops here for a person to look at.
demo.approved: APPROVED · Your approval is bound to the target, operation and revision shown, so the request clears the gate and the flow runs to the end. Nothing real was touched.
demo.allowed: ALLOWED · This exact request now has authority, so the flow runs to the end. Nothing real was touched.
demo.invalidated: APPROVAL REVOKED · The request changed, so the previous approval is void — even if you set the values back to what they were.
demo.evidence: Illustrative evidence: identity workflow-agent-17, the target and revision, the policy decision, and what the approval actually covered. After a real action you still compare what happened against what was approved, and reconcile any difference.
demo.static: A restart of production/payment-api by workflow-agent-17, which is authorized only for staging/*, is refused. A human approval naming that target, the restart operation and revision 182 permits that one request and nothing else. Identity and permissions come from the execution layer, never from what the model claims about itself.

home.title: Infrastructure engineering & governed AI in Thailand
home.description: Nearly 20 years in enterprise infrastructure, enabling Thailand's leading SI partners. Architecture, migration, private AI, and AI your organization can actually keep under control.
home.headline: AI your organization can actually rely on.
home.lede: Nearly 20 years in enterprise infrastructure. We connect AI to the systems you already run, and we make sure it can only do what it is allowed to do.

sections.title: A prompt is not a control.
sections.body: Writing do not delete anything into an instruction does not make deletion impossible. It is a request, and a system that works on probability is free to ignore it. No organization can run on the hope that the model behaves itself. What an AI is allowed to do has to be enforced outside the model, in a layer it cannot talk its way past.

sections.title: Fit the business. Make authority explicit.
sections.body: AI that works with your business, inside limits you can point at.

items.title: Use the systems you already have
items.body: You do not rebuild anything to suit us. We connect to the systems, data, identities and approvals your organization already runs on.

items.title: Nothing is permitted by default
items.body: Every agent has a named identity, its own permissions and a defined scope. Claiming authority in a prompt does not create it.

items.title: People stay in charge
items.body: Approved routine work runs on its own. Risk, doubt and anything unusual goes to the person who is accountable for it.

sections.title: From infrastructure decisions to systems that run.

items.title: Infrastructure & migration

items.title: Private AI & governed workflows

items.title: SI partner enablement

sections.title: Decision-makers should look at what actually needs them.
sections.body: AI takes the work that costs time and labour. People check the parts that matter. The system has to put complete, short evidence in front of the reviewer — not let AI run unchecked.

items.title: Normal result
items.body: Continues inside the approved workflow.

items.title: High value, missing evidence or conflicting data
items.body: Stops for a person to review.

items.title: Low confidence
items.body: Escalates the doubt instead of inventing certainty.

items.title: Against policy
items.body: Blocks the action and asks for review.

items.title: Wide blast radius
items.body: Requires explicit approval before anything runs.

sections.body: Work with a principal engineer on the decisions that shape reliability, operability and the path to production.

items.title: Architecture & migration
items.body: Assess the platform, map the dependencies and compare container, virtualization and private-cloud options. You get architecture decisions, a phased migration plan, validation criteria and a rollback position.

items.title: Private AI infrastructure
items.body: Plan the compute, model serving, data access, identity and who operates it. Weigh local, enterprise-hosted and approved API options against what the workload actually needs, rather than a favourite model.

sections.title: Four ways to connect AI to the business.
sections.body: Light provides the control and execution foundation. The engagement adapts it to your data, identities, systems and approval steps.

items.title: Enterprise AI Workflow Engineering
items.body: Turn an existing process into an AI-assisted one: connect the authoritative data, define the reasoning task, structure the output and place the human checkpoints. It applies to finance, procurement, compliance, operations, support, sales operations, manufacturing, logistics, documents, reporting and IT.

items.title: Governed Agent Operations
items.body: Give each workload a durable identity, its own authorization, scoped tool access and defined limits on what it may change. Wire in human approval, policy checks, audit and after-the-fact reconciliation. The model proposes; the platform decides whether it runs.

items.title: Service & Dependency Intelligence
items.body: Build a service graph out of real evidence from repositories, configuration, runtime, infrastructure and documentation. Find dependencies and owners, spot changes, judge blast radius, prepare impact reports and support migrations and incident investigation.

items.title: Custom Enterprise AI Solution
items.body: Design a bounded solution around your own data and way of working when packaged software does not fit. Prepare the context, reason, produce structured output, validate it, and return the result to the existing workflow through a human or policy boundary.

sections.title: Built for the whole organization, not a pilot for six people.
sections.body: The same controlled foundation carries very different workloads. What changes is the data and the approvals — not the way authority is enforced.

items.title: Chatbot
items.body: An assistant the entire company can ask, not a demo a handful of people try once. It answers from real internal information, and it knows which questions each person is allowed to have answered.

items.title: RAG
items.body: Answers drawn from your own documents, with a citation back to the source it used — so a reviewer can check the answer instead of having to trust it.

items.title: GraphRAG
items.body: Connects relationships across systems and documents, so the questions that need several hops can be answered at all: who depends on this, and what breaks if we change it.

sections.title: AI workflows need maintenance, not just a launch.
sections.body: Review the corrections people made, the outputs they rejected, the escalations and exceptions, the false positives and negatives, how long things take, how the model performs, and what changed in the data and the business rules. AI can propose improvements, but every change is tested, reviewed and released as a controlled revision. Production policy never changes quietly.

platform.title: Light: the control layer for enterprise AI
platform.description: Separate flexible AI reasoning from controlled execution. Connect Light to your enterprise systems, private models and frontier APIs, with authority enforced outside the model.
platform.headline: Flexible reasoning. Strict control.
platform.lede: Light is the control and execution layer for AI. It governs a system that works on probability so the results can be trusted. It does not pretend to turn a language model into a deterministic one.

sections.title: Keep model choice separate from authority.
sections.body: Agents can run on local, enterprise-hosted or frontier models. Light governs identity, authorization, scope, approval, tool access, state, audit, execution and reconciliation before any of them reach your systems.

sections.kicker: Why a prompt is not enough
sections.title: Enforcement has to live outside the model.
sections.body: An instruction is a request. A permission is a fact. Three things have to be true outside the model for the difference to hold.

items.title: Instructions are requests, not limits
items.body: A model can ignore a rule in its prompt, misread it, or be argued out of it. Nothing written in a prompt is a boundary, however firmly it is worded.

items.title: Permissions sit outside the model
items.body: Identity, scope and approval are checked by the execution layer. The model can ask for something; it cannot grant itself anything.

items.title: Every action leaves evidence
items.body: What was requested, what the policy decided, who approved it and what actually happened are all recorded, so somebody can check afterwards.

sections.title: Flexible data. Unambiguous control.
sections.body: Information specific to one customer should not mean rebuilding the platform. Combine known control fields with flexible business payloads, evidence, reasoning instructions and structured output.

items.title: Controlled structured fields
items.body: Authorization, routing, enforcement, thresholds and state changes use explicit structured data. A sentence inside a business document does not grant permission.

items.title: Flexible business payload
items.body: Documents, text and JSON carry the context of the job. Their evidence and instructions stay separate from the control fields the platform trusts.

items.title: Validated output
items.body: Check structured output against what the workflow expects, then apply the human or policy boundary before it returns to an existing process.

sections.title: Use the model that fits the work.
sections.body: Choose on security, capability, performance and cost. The control model stays the same across providers, and no single model is best at everything.

items.title: Local / private models
items.body: An option for sensitive data, within your own data controls and whatever your team can realistically operate.

items.title: Enterprise-hosted AI
items.body: Controlled serving and access for workloads that belong on your enterprise platform.

items.title: Frontier APIs
items.body: An option for genuinely hard reasoning, when your data policy allows an external service.

items.title: Smaller models
items.body: Worth evaluating for classification, extraction and routine processing, where a large model earns nothing.

governance.title: AI governance: explicit identity, scope & human approval
governance.description: See a scoped agent request refused, watch the flow stop at the approval gate, and see why AI identity cannot simply be claimed in a prompt.
governance.headline: The model proposes. Something else decides.
governance.lede: AI can reason freely. Touching real systems cannot be free. Identity, permissions and approval come from the execution layer — not from what the model says about itself.

sections.title: Staging authority does not include production.
sections.body: The same proposed action can be useful and still not be allowed. The policy decision happens before execution, not afterwards — so the flow stops and waits for a person.

sections.title: Check the request. Keep the evidence.
sections.body: Defining the controls for each workflow is part of the integration work, including how to stop something and who is allowed to approve an exception.

items.title: Identity & authorization
items.body: Trusted workload identity and explicit permissions. A model does not inherit another agent's authority by claiming to be it.

items.title: Scope & approval
items.body: Tool access and changes are bound to an approved target, operation and revision. If the intent changes, the approval has to be given again.

items.title: State & audit
items.body: Record the request, the policy decision, the approval and the outcome, so a reviewer can reconstruct what was allowed and what happened.

items.title: Verify & reconcile
items.body: Compare what actually happened against what was approved. Surface partial failures, unexpected changes and unresolved outcomes to someone who can act on them.

sections.title: Send people the cases that genuinely need a person.
sections.body: AI handles the volume; people handle the judgment. What gets escalated is written down as a rule, so nobody is asked to trust a confidence score without seeing the evidence behind it.

items.title: Normal result
items.body: Runs under the policy already approved.

items.title: High-value transaction
items.body: Always goes to a person.

items.title: Missing evidence or conflicting data
items.body: Stops and asks someone accountable.

items.title: Low confidence
items.body: Escalates instead of guessing.

items.title: Against policy
items.body: Blocked, then routed to review.

items.title: Wide blast radius
items.body: Needs explicit approval first.

how-we-work.title: How we work: understand, integrate, govern & improve
how-we-work.description: An infrastructure-led engagement with clear outcomes, authoritative evidence, integration, human approval boundaries and controlled production changes.
how-we-work.headline: A system that works starts with a shared understanding.
how-we-work.lede: We carry the integration work. Your team keeps the business decisions, the operating responsibility and the authority to say what AI may do.

sections.title: Agree the outcome and the boundaries first.
sections.body: Scope the work around your environment. Settle what gets delivered, and how it will be checked, before anything gets built.

items.title: Understand
items.body: Identify the outcome you want, the evidence it needs, where the authoritative data lives, what may be decided and acted on, and what stays with people. Map the infrastructure and workflow you have now.

items.title: Integrate
items.body: Connect systems, APIs, databases, documents, infrastructure, identity and the workflows already in use. Prepare context from real evidence and return validated results into the process people actually work in.

items.title: Govern
items.body: Define agent identity, permissions, scope, approval gates, escalation, validation and audit requirements. Test the paths that must be refused as carefully as the ones that must succeed.

items.title: Operate & improve
items.body: Check the results in production, hand over the operating knowledge, and review corrections and exceptions. Changes are tested, reviewed and released as explicit workflow revisions.

sections.title: Reasoning is only one part of the workflow.
sections.body: The same pattern covers IT operations and business processes. Data arrives as evidence; it never turns into authority.

items.title: Enterprise data
items.body: Use authoritative sources.

items.title: Context preparation
items.body: Select the relevant evidence.

items.title: AI reasoning
items.body: Follow explicit instructions.

items.title: Structured output
items.body: Produce a defined result.

items.title: Validation
items.body: Check the result and its evidence.

items.title: Human / policy boundary
items.body: Check permission before acting.

items.title: Existing workflow
items.body: Integrate, verify and reconcile.

sections.title: Your systems. Your judgment. Clear ownership.
sections.body: Put AI into a real business workflow. Give each agent only the authority its role actually needs. Work with systems and processes your organization already trusts. Verify, govern and audit what AI is permitted to do. Automation should make your people more capable, not quietly remove them from decisions they are answerable for.
